title: Trust in Mind - Part 1
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up the opening lines of the Xinxinming (Trust in Mind) by Sengcan, "The true way is without difficulty, just avoid picking and choosing," and follows them through four Zhaozhou cases in the Blue Cliff Record. Norman traces suffering to grasping and rejecting, then offers equanimity as the way to meet each moment as it is. In case 57, Zhaozhou answers a monastic with the baby Buddha's words, then gets angry at the monastic's disrespect for himself. In case 59, Zhaozhou tells a monk who recalls only one line of the poem that the line is enough. Norman closes with a story in which one sits, one stands, and each sees the other.

sentences.text: Good morning, everybody.
I'm really happy for myself; I'm happy that I have arrived again at our precious samish sesshin.
It's great to be here.
This is a wonderful assembly of bodhisattvas.
I apologize for being late, but the advantage of being late is that you arrive and everybody's all ready.
It's beautiful; I can feel your strength.
This morning I want to bring up a really important teaching of our tradition, a basic teaching about how we are going to live with our unruly minds.
I'm sure many of you will be familiar with this teaching; it's the opening lines of the *Shen Shen Ming*, trust in mind, composed by the third Zhen ancestor in China, a sensei.
The poem is usually *Shen Shen Ming*, which is translated as trust in mind.
Here, mind means not just our mental faculties, but a big mind—the all-inclusive mind of reality, which we usually call for shorthand Buddha.
And the word trust in the title means trust or faith or confidence in this mind as being who we actually are and how we actually live.
So I think we're all very aware.
We know it from our sitting, but we don't have to sit to be aware of how much our mind is full of turmoil, prejudice, confusion, and all sorts of pain.
So even though we all have absolute faith in our own opinions, when you look a little bit more, you think, "Why would I have faith in that?"
It's very shaky being oneself.
And yet, behind and underneath and through and through, this confused mind is true mind, Buddha mind.
That's wonderful news; we don't have to make a Buddha mind where there isn't one already.
It's there.
So the question is, how do we locate it and how do we learn how to trust it?
This is what *Shen Shen Ming* is about.
And the opening lines of the poem are very famous: *The true way is without difficulty, just avoid picking and choosing.

When you don't grasp or reject the way, it enlightens itself.* This is maybe like the basic Buddhist teaching at the very beginning: *All condition existence is marked by suffering.* What's the cause of this suffering?
Grasping and rejecting.
If only you could let go of grasping and rejecting, then everything would immediately become very simple.
There wouldn't be any more suffering, and true mind would just appear as an everyday affair right in front of you all the time.
Things would just be as they are.

The Buddha tried to describe the details of how suffering unfolds in our hearts, and he did this by talking about the 12-fold chain of causation, which describes how suffering unfolds and feeds on itself like a snake chasing its own tail.

When he said that whenever there was contact between a sense organ and a sense object in the mind, whenever there was this contact, where it could be between a thought and emotion inside in the mind, there was contact.
At that point of contact, there's always what he called *vedanā*, usually translated as feeling or sensation that's always there; there's any human experience.
And the nature of *vedanā* is exactly clinging and rejecting.
So when we pay attention, we really see clinging and rejecting runs far deeper than we thought it did; it's very subtle.
And the more you practice zazen, the more you see this.
You hear about clinging and grasping in the dharma talk or you read about it in the book, and it sort of makes you pay attention to it.
And you observe it in yourself.
And you see that all the time when you're on your cushion or on your cushion, there's always on every moment some clinging and rejecting.
Sometimes a lot, and then you're suffering a lot and you're really miserable, and you know it, although you can't seem to stop.
Sometimes not so much, and then you tend to ignore it.
But if you look, you see that it's there.
And then you begin to get the idea that if you are alive in the world, there's always going to be some grasping and rejecting because you would rather live than die, wouldn't you?
I like life; I don't like death.
I would rather live than die.
And from that everything flows—all the clinging and all the rejecting don't show this basic impulse that we don't even think about.
Of course, Sengsan in writing his poem understands this.
So when he writes, "just avoid picking and choosing," "just avoid grasping and rejecting," what is he talking about?
He must mean that we can accept and live our human situation in a radically different way.

That there must be a way of grasping and rejecting in the spirit of not grasping and rejecting so that when you're caught by your grasping and rejecting, there must be a way of not being caught by the grasping and rejecting that may be present.
And then when you're not caught by the grasping and rejecting, there is no grasping and rejecting.
I think that's what he means.
Anyway, we chant the Heart Sutra all the time.
And if we pay any attention, we realize there isn't anything to grasp or reject, right?
Isn't that what it says?
*Our discriminative consciousness is based on a fundamental fallacy, on a projection, on a big illusion.
It's based on an apparent separation between object and subject.
The mind that perceives on one side and the perceived object on the other side appear to us to be two different independent things.
But that's not true.
There really isn't any real distinction between mind and object, which you can observe if you pay attention.
Mind and object arise together as a single reality.*
Look at your mind.
There's always something there.
Nothing there, no mind.
And without the mind, there's nothing there for you.
So there is no real fundamental distinction between mind and object.
Mind and object arise together as one reality, depending on each other so completely that they are, in fact, like that.
And our everyday reality does not appreciate this basic fact of life.
As Vasubandhu teaches us in his texts about mind, everyday reality, as we know it, is imaginary.
It is unreal.
And as human beings, we naturally need to live real lives in order to be healthy.
And when our lives are not real, when they're unreal, something is wrong.
Something is off.
And we feel that.
Buddha referred to this as dis-ease, *dukkha*.
To be human in the ordinary way is to be dis-eased.
Deep down, we know something is missing.
Something isn't right.
And we long for wholeness.
And practice is the path of wholeness, the path of belonging.
As the sutra says, *things are empty of separation, which means they're boundless.
They have no boundaries.
You can't grasp something without a boundary.
You can't reject something without beginning or end.
And you can't hold on to your life and avoid your death.* And yet we all insist on the impossible, moment after moment.
You can't even hold on to a single instant of your life.
Not a single instant, wonderful as it may be.
You can't hold on to it.
Nor can you make a single instant of your life go away while it is here.
Things come and go as they will.
Nobody can stop them.
So why cling and reject?
According to Buddha, it is absolutely vital to really embrace this point if you want to have some happiness and some peace of mind, and also, not incidentally, to feel some compassion.
Because compassion is total acceptance.
Compassion is going beyond grasping and rejecting.
And this is the lucidity and the clarity that Seng San is talking about in his poem.
When you appreciate what's really real and can go beyond your grasping and rejecting, then awakening is right there.
And the peace, the love, and the wisdom that we seek is right in front of us.
I think another way of understanding what Seng San is teaching here is to see that he's asking us to practice equanimity.
To allow every moment of our lives to be as it is without complaining and without attachment.
And there is no other way.
Like they used to say, "Why fight city hall?"
There's no other way.
Take a breath.
Return to presence.
And just see through your prejudices and appreciate everything, even if you don't like it.
Why do you have to like it?
What's the difference anyway, really?
Whether you like it or not, is it that important, really?
Whether you like it or not?
What's important is what actually occurs, not what you think should have occurred.
What you think is supposed to be is very, very flimsy stuff compared to the awesome fact of what is right here, right now.
And equanimity is knowing that and being able to really appreciate things the way they are.
The Pali word for equanimity, *upekha*, *upeksha* in Sanskrit means, etymologically, "take a closer look."
See things just as they are, without your prejudices and your desires and your needs, so-called needs in the way.
In the classical teachings, the mind of equanimity is described as a mind that is pliable, stable, flexible, not fluttering, concentrated, pure, clean, honest.
And isn't this the kind of mind that is demonstrated over and over again in the stories of the ancients?
These old Zen teachers are very open and flexible.
They can jump this way or that way according to conditions.
They don't stick to anything.
They're not blinded by their ideas.
Like they say, they have room to turn around.
And because of this, they could be very kind and very wise.
And because they were equanimous, they were not moved at all by clinging or rejecting, even though they were human.
And so they had their likes and dislikes just like the human else.
When you practice equanimity, though, the likes and the dislikes quiet down quite a bit.
You realize how much you were identifying with your likes and dislikes and clinging to them as if you were clinging to your very life.
And when you loosen up, your likes and dislikes also loosen up, and some of them just disappear.
And your way of looking at things changes quite a lot.
You don't any longer love one and hate the other because you have a love that's bigger than that, that doesn't require that.
That includes everything equally.
And there's absolutely nothing that could happen that would violate that love because equanimity also means a mind of equality.
And when you let go of clinging and rejecting, you see things with a mind of equality.
Each one, each happening is okay because it must be this way.
If it is this way, it couldn't be another way.
This is not at all resignation to fate.
This was the most revolutionary aspect of the Buddhist teaching.
One does not have to resign oneself to fate; one never need feel helpless.
Because when we are practicing, every moment we are planting seeds of goodness that will make the future brighter.

So it's not fatalism, but it does mean that right now in this unrepeatable and ungraspable moment, things are as they are, and we can accept them because we understand them and we know where they come from.
Zhaozhou liked to quote Shengshan in his opening lines in the Blue Cliff Record, case two, second story.
He does that.
He begins by saying, *The true way is not difficulty, just avoid picking and choosing.* And then he says, *As soon as there are words, there is picking and choosing or there is clarity.
But I don't have that clarity.* Do you appreciate the meaning of this, he says to the assembled monastics?
And one of them comes forward and says, "Since you don't have that clarity, how do you appreciate the meaning of this?"
And Zhaozhou says, "I don't know."
And the monastic says, "Well, since you don't know, how can you say you don't have that clarity?"
And Zhaozhou says, "Good question.
Please bow and go away."
We love Zhaozhou; he's so subtle with his words.
As we were just saying, we see by observation that consciousness, whenever it appears, especially in our language, always involves discrimination.
And that's why it would appear sometimes that the Zen masters are trying to warn us away from language.
But here, surprisingly, Zhaozhou says that when words appear, there can be discrimination, but there can also be freedom, which is surprising, he says that.
So he's saying, yeah, language certainly can be a trap.
We get so caught by our ideas, our concepts, our words, but also words can free you, he says.
How could that be?
It must be because you understand the words very differently.
And that's how we understand Zen stories, very differently than the usual way of understanding.
We have an ungraspable feeling for the language of these stories.
Then he says, "I don't have that freedom."
Why would he say that?
Because he doesn't have that freedom.
He isn't caught in the language trap in which as soon as you say you're free or think you're free, you're immediately bound by what?
By that concept of freedom.
There really isn't any freedom or bondage; there's just what is, neither free nor bound, or both free and bound, equanimity, things as they are.
So then Zhaozhou turns to the sangha, "How do you appreciate this teaching?"
And the monastic says, "What about you?
How do you appreciate it?"
And he says, "I don't understand it."
The monastic says, "But isn't that the understanding we're after?"

This is pretty smart monastic, pretty nervy and quick on her feet, but seems to still not be able to get over the idea that surely Zhaozhou has achieved something, or maybe she thinks she's achieved something, or maybe she thinks there's something she should be achieving that she hasn't yet achieved.
And Zhaozhou says, "Good question.
Bow and go away."
Keep asking the question.
Dogen always says this, and here it seems like Zhaozhou is saying the same thing.
The goal of our practice really is not awakening.

Awakening, if we think awakening is some kind of serenity and clarity beyond discrimination, that's just another word to describe another state of mind among the many coming and going states of mind in the lifetime.
Just one more thing to grasp or reject.
If we experience awakening and affirm it and identify with it and identify it as a thing, we have already been grasping and clinging.
We're already caught.
And if we have it and then we lose it, we can hardly wait to get it back.
And then we go shopping.

We go to the spiritual marketplace, hoping to find the latest teacher or teaching, the latest app or product that will bring us back to our desired state and out of our undesired state, which will become more and more painful with our rejection and denial of it.
That's the opposite of equanimity.
Like all good Zen teachers, Zhaozhou does not have a plan or a program.
He is not an expert at being human.
At being human.
He just is human.
I don't know either, he says.
But he's willing to live his life and see what happens with wonder, with humility, side by side with everybody else and exactly like everybody else.

And he says this in the most matter of fact way, not as some great spiritual accomplishment, but simply as the way we human beings, all of us, every single one of us, are capable of living and want to live that way.
There's nothing special about this at all.
We human beings appear anyway to have the capacity for autonomy and free will.
We appear to be able to override our instinct if we decide to do so.
So in each moment of ordinary activity and thought, we discriminate on what basis?
Well, we discriminate on the basis of our karma, our personal situations, our training, our conditioning.
Not only that, we also can discriminate on the basis of our spiritual training and our commitment to precepts.
The moment after moment, every choice that we make will be both right and wrong because reality has a tragic quality to it.
You cannot pick up anything without causing some harm and you can't live any moment without being one moment closer to the end of your life.
And at the same time, everything we pick up will have some benefit and every moment lived will be a moment of appreciation and profound learning, almost an eternal moment throughout the cosmos.
Whatever we get and lose, we can accept in that moment.
And when we do, it will be a new moment.
Anyway, we will be at the end of every moment in a brand new situation.
If we can live like that, we can know a true and lasting human happiness.

And if we're lucky enough, as we're all lucky here, to be able to practice shun and possibly have moments of deep serenity, we don't get too excited about it because we know that every moment, beautiful or ugly, is a passing moment.
And when we know that, we enjoy those moments of tranquility and insight even more.
And as we practice letting go of all moments, moments of tranquility and insight actually increase in frequency and they're not such a big deal.
In fact, the more that we know this teaching in our very bones, the more every moment has this flavor.
Even a tough moment is illuminating.
Actually, the Blue Cliff Record has four stories, four different stories out of the 100 stories of the Blue Cliff Record, each time differently depending on the conditions.
Because I think he understood it differently every time.
In the 57th story, a monastic says, *the ultimate path has no difficulties, just avoid picking and choosing*.
What is not picking and choosing?
And Zhaozhou says, *in the heavens above and in the earth below, I alone am the world-honored one*.
And this monastic, think of the chutzpah this monastic says to him, isn't that still picking and choosing?
And Zhaozhou says, you idiot, where is the picking and choosing, which left the monastic speechless.
So this time the monastic is emphasizing the basic point that we've been talking about, that there's always discrimination.
There's no avoiding it as long as we're alive.
And the more we look at it, the more painful it gets.
I always say to people, practice actually makes your life worse.
It's true.
Anybody who practiced a long time would say, oh, I was much better off.
I knew I was screwed up, but I didn't realize the extent of it until I began to practice.

Now that you practice for a while, stuff that you did every day that you completely took for granted and never minded at all, stuff like squashing bugs, belittling other people when you tell jokes, favoring yourself all the time over other people without even thinking about it, trashing your body and mind because you didn't have time to pay attention.
All that stuff that you cheerfully were able to do before without worrying about it.
Now you find it very painful and it's frustrating that you can't stop doing it.
Even the very fact of being alive and doing well in an unjust world, which now we recognize, we say we have a word for that, we're privileged, even that is painful.
And this monastic is saying, isn't that how it is and there's nothing we can do.
Anyway, he's asking, he's putting this to Zhaozhou.
Zhaozhou answers him by quoting the words that in Zen tradition we say that the Buddha said right after he was born, the Buddha was not a regular kid, a regular baby.

If you have a baby, I very much doubt your baby will do what the Buddha did, which is immediately pop out of the womb, take seven steps forward, put one finger up, pointing to the heavens and one finger down pointing to the earth and said, *and the heavens above and the earth below, I am*.
Which is why the baby Buddha statue looks like that.
That's what the Buddha said, *in the heavens above and the earth below, I alone in the world*.
And Zhaozhou in quoting these words is basically saying, our very picking and choosing is Buddha.
Every moment, everything that happens is Buddha.
Even the pain, even the sorrow.
Every choice we make is as it must be.
If that's so, is there any picking and choosing at all?
Did any of us ever pick and choose anything?
But then the monastic says, but isn't that already picking and choosing?
And it seems from the story that Zhaozhou actually lost him.
He got mad at this monastic.
And he got mad at him for the one good reason to get mad at somebody.
There's one really good reason for the fact.
How can you disrespect yourself so profoundly?
How can you treat yourself like that?
How can you fail to see who you really are?
How can you take this precious human life that you've been given for reasons you will never understand and treat it as if it were something small and mean and worthless?
That's how come Zhaozhou gets mad at this monastic.
And the monastic feeling, the passion of Zhaozhou's concern is rendered speechless.
The very next story is another one, 58.
The monastic says, *the ultimate path has no difficulties, just avoid picking and choosing*.
Isn't this a cliche?
Now Zhaozhou says, once someone asked me about this, and I couldn't explain for five years, teachings do become cliches.
I say to people, if you ask the AI robot a darn question, it's guaranteed that you'll get a better answer from the AI robot than from any Dharma teacher on the planet.
Because the AI robot knows what all the Dharma teachers know.
Every Dharma teacher only knows what they know.
Spiritual teachings do become cliches, easy to mix and match them and spit them out.
I've been studying these old cases for many decades and I've gotten used to them, but also I never get used to them.
Every time I study one, I always begin with the feeling that I really don't know what this means.
I have no idea what this story is trying to tell me.
And I recommend that you too don't get too familiar with religious teachings and think you know what they mean.
Don't ever think that.
The worst thing that anybody could become is a religious professional.
You don't want to become a professional.
We should all be amateurs.
Even having values and principles gets in the way.
We're often blinded.
We don't see what's in front of us.
Even our good motivations and our positive intentions can become problems.
Suzuki Roshi always says, not always so.
Maybe it was so before.
Maybe it's even so right now.
But that doesn't mean it'll be so always.
Right or wrong.
Good or bad.
This is it.
So every time someone asks Zhaozhou about picking and choosing, he has to start all over again from the beginning.
This time he says, yeah, they asked me about this and I thought it over for five years and I couldn't figure it out.
Maybe you couldn't figure it out in a hundred years.
Maybe if you could figure it out and explain it perfectly well, that would not be such a good thing.
The next story, the 59th story, the monastic asks Zhaozhou, *the ultimate path has no difficulties, just avoid picking and choosing*.
As soon as there are words and speech, there is picking and choosing.
So how do you help anybody?
Zhaozhou said to the monastic, quote the whole poem.
The monastic said, well, I only remember that line.
And Zhaozhou said, that line is enough.
*The ultimate path has no difficulties, just avoid picking and choosing*.
So the monastic is bringing up a really good point.
Compassion.
How do you help anybody?
How does sitting on our cushions here and contemplating Zen words do any good for anyone?
So I remind us all that we are not sitting here for our personal edification.

We're sitting here because we are really and literally in the midst of a desperate situation and we are trying to save ourselves and to help as far as we can our brothers and sisters who are in the same desperate situation that we are in.
But how exactly does this help?
Zhaozhou seems to ignore the question entirely.
And he says to the monk, quote the whole poem, the poem is 146 four character lines long, runs to five or six pages in English translation.
And the monk doesn't remember it.
Maybe he had it memorized at one point, but he doesn't remember it right now.
And Zhaozhou says, no need.
You just need the one line.
But you need this line not as something to memorize and recite, but as something to embody and live.
Come back to yourself in each moment of discrimination.
From your sesshin practice, from your Zhaozhou practice every day, learn how to do that immediately as the way you respond moment after moment to conditions.
When you can do that, there is equanimity.
When there is equanimity, there is clear seeing.
When you can see clearly, you always know how to help.
Forget the poem.
Just be your life.
Be ready all the time.
Give yourself plenty of room to turn around it.
Be a human being.
That will be help enough for everyone.
One more story.
This one is from Manasho Dogen, collected 300 Zen stories.
And this is the 11th one.
In this case, Zhaozhou doesn't quote the first lines, he quotes the very next lines, which say, *if you have even a little bit of discrimination, the mind is lost in confusion*.
And he says to the assembled monastics, what do you say about this?
And oddly, one of them whacks Zhaozhou's attendant.
Like, if you like, whacking me, me sitting there whacking your business.
And then the person, me sitting there whacking your business.
And then the person, whacks me.
Zhaozhou witnesses this and leaves.
He goes away.
And the attendant goes with him and says, what was that?
Does Razalyn know what she's talking about or not?
And Zhaozhou answers, *the one who sits, sees the one who stands.
The one who stands, sees the one who sits*.
So that's it.
We sit, then we are the sitting person.
We stand, now we're the standing person.
We walk, now we're the walking person.
Because we see and hear and think, we see difference.
And we don't.
And we understand.
And we don't.
We open our eyes and we see one another.
True.
In seeing one another, we see ourselves.
Because the only way you can really see yourself is to see the other.
And as soon as we disrespect one another, we disrespect ourselves, our true nature.
And then we distort our human heart and you can see what happens.
And yet, we do that.
Little by little by little, we are learning to do better.
And we keep trying to practice.
And we observe our heart and our mind.
And our practice is successful.
And it's not.
But it doesn't matter.
Because we're walking straight ahead.
And we keep on going.
This is a full, honest, realistic, and joyful life.
Thank you all very much for listening to my talk.
I don't take it for granted.
I really appreciate it.
And more than that, thank you for your practice so far in this sesshin and in the days to come.
Take care of yourself.
See what's going on.

This is a wonderful assembly of bodhisattvas. I apologize for being late. But the advantage of being late is that you arrive and everybody's all ready. It's beautiful. I can feel your strength. This morning I want to bring up a really important teaching of our tradition, a basic teaching about how we are going to live with our unruly minds. I'm sure many of you will be familiar with this teaching. It's the opening lines of the shen shen ming, trust in mind, composed by the third zhen ancestor in China,

a sensei. The poem is usually shen shen ming, which is translated as trust in mind. And here mind means not just our mental faculties, but a big mind, the mind, the all-inclusive mind of reality, which we usually call for shorthand buddha. And you observe it in

yourself. And you see that all the time when you're on your cushion or on your cushion, there's always on every moment some clinging and rejecting. Sometimes a lot and then you're suffering a lot and you're really miserable and you know it, although you can't seem to stop. Sometimes not so much and then you tend to ignore it. But if you look, you see that it's there. And then you begin to get the idea that if you are alive in the world, there's always going to be some grasping and rejecting because you would rather live than die, wouldn't you? I like life. I don't like death. I would rather live than die. And from that everything flows. All the clinging and all the rejecting

don't show this basic impulse that we don't even think about. Now, of course, Sengson in writing his poem understands this. So when he writes, just avoid picking and choosing, just avoid grasping and rejecting, what is he talking about? He must mean that we can accept and live our human situation in a radically different way. That there must be a way of grasping and rejecting in the spirit of not grasping and rejecting so that when you're caught by your grasping and rejecting, there must be a way of not being caught by the grasping and rejecting that may be present. And then when you're not caught by the grasping and rejecting, there is no grasping and rejecting. I think that's what he

means. And anyway, we chant the Heart Sutra all the time. And if we pay any attention, we realize there isn't anything to grasp or reject, right? Isn't that what it says? Our discriminative consciousness is based on a fundamental fallacy, on a projection, on a big illusion. It's based on an apparent separation between object and subject.
